commit.message:
qa: a cleared auction must not offer to bid on or re-clear itself

Both revert AlreadyCleared, so the control being there is an offer to pay for a
transaction that cannot succeed. Cheap half of the demo-row lesson: a button
that should not be there costs as much as a guard that does not fire.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: the no-funds check no longer depends on the wallet staying broke

It posted a 5 FXRP lot from a wallet that held nothing and asserted the desk
said so. Today's settlements paid that wallet 5.1 FXRP — it is a published test
key on a public testnet, so its balance is nobody's to control — and the desk
correctly stopped refusing. The check reported "no pre-flight message", which
points at the page for something the page got right.

It now reads the balance and asks for one whole FXRP more than that, so the
refusal is the only correct answer whatever the wallet holds.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

two things a judge trips over in the first minute

`npm run pay -- --help` answered with `"--help" is not a destination tag` and
exit 2. The usage text was right there underneath, so the information was
correct and the verdict was wrong — the first command anyone types should not
look like a failure. It prints usage and exits 0 now, and each flag says what it
is for. A genuinely bad tag still fails the same way it did.

And the executor report said `won 0` while the submission cites a race this bot
won. Both are true — the ledger is this machine's memory of what it did, and a
fresh checkout has none — but read together they look like a contradiction, and
the reader has no reason to guess which one is lying. It now says so, and points
at `npm run status`, which reads the chain.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: the claim parser reads a linked address as an address

Adding explorer links to the seven bare addresses broke five checks into
"SUBMISSION.md still names AssetManagerFXRP — the line is gone". The document
was fine; the patterns were anchored on a bare code span, so a formatting change
reported as a missing claim. That is the second time today an anchor did this,
which is the argument for anchoring on the label rather than the shape.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: three checks that were not checking anything

hostile-operator.mjs needed a desk started by hand — one vite, one env var, one
port — and without it every case navigated to nothing and reported "blank page".
Ten hostile payloads, ten failures, none of them about the desk. It starts the
desk itself now, and all ten pass.

qa:visual:desk pointed at localhost:4192, which nothing serves, so it died on a
navigation timeout. Pointed at the built bundle it then diffed 100% on every
viewport: visual.mjs served /dashboard/ by falling through to the ROOT
index.html, so the desk's baselines were being compared against the landing
page. A directory resolves to its own index.html now, --path= reaches a page
that is not at the root, and the desk baselines are real desk screenshots.
qa:visual runs all three.

docs.test.ts asserted /0x20d9…|undelayed/ against a document with the word
"undelayed" throughout, so the address half could never fail. It now requires
every address the submission states to have an explorer link behind it — which
found seven that did not.

And the desk suite gained the one check that guards the most expensive bug this
project has had: pressing a row-scoped on-chain button on the demo book must ask
the wallet for nothing. Disabling rowIsReal makes it fail with one signing
request, so it bites. Finding that took fixing a second thing — "an enclave
replied" was true for any 200 on /direct, and a static server's SPA fallback
answers 200 with HTML.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: the desk's extension id comes from the desk's own config

The audit-panel check asks the diamond which contract is bound to the extension
and compares it with what the page prints. The id was pinned here, so the day
buta redeployed to extension 66009 the check read the retired extension's sender
and reported the live page as wrong — a false failure that points at the page
instead of at itself.

It reads ../buta/config/extension.env now, which is what buta's deploy writes,
and EXT_ID= overrides it for a target that is not the sibling checkout.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: screenshots follow the file, not the working directory

render.mjs defaulted its shot directory to the literal "qa/shots", which is
only correct when it is run from the repo root. Run it from inside qa/ and it
writes qa/qa/shots — a path .gitignore does not cover, because that rule is
anchored at the root — so throwaway screenshots show up as untracked files and
read like something worth committing. Resolved from import.meta.url now, the
same way pageDir already was.

Also ignore .vercel, which the dashboard deploy leaves behind.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: the test wallet can broadcast, but only when a driver asks it to

buta's scripts/settle-from-browser.mjs is committed and imports this file with
{ broadcast: true }. Without the option it landed here uncommitted, so a clean
clone of undelayed gave that script a wallet that refuses to send — the one
thing it exists to do.

The refusal stays the default, and stays the right default for suites: a check
that spends real gas is a check nobody runs twice, which is the same as no
check at all. The exception is narrow and deliberate. Settling from the actual
page is the only way to test the desk rather than the libraries the desk and
the node scripts share, and that proof cost four bugs that no node run could
have found.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: two suites were pointed at a directory that had moved

`qa:visual` and `qa:flows` both targeted ../buta/landing. The landing page is
at ../buta/frontend/landing and has been for a while. The local server answers
a missing path with a 404 and Playwright screenshots that as a blank page, so
the landing baselines diffed at 100% against every viewport — which reads as
"the page changed completely" rather than "the path is wrong". flows.mjs failed
the same way, as `waiting for locator('#usd')`, which points at the page
instead of at the command.

Both now refuse a target with no index.html rather than comparing against
whatever a 404 renders as.

And the desk's pre-flight is checked from the browser: a connected wallet
holding no FXRP gets a sentence naming what it holds, and no signature request
for a transaction that would revert. It needed the reserve field filled to get
that far — without it the desk stops earlier, correctly, and the check was
passing through a door it never opened.

The sharpest test of the whole claim: seal a bid against an operator that

qa: the hostile server answers per command, so both read paths are covered

It replied with the book to every poll, which meant the receipt cases were
really testing the book again. It remembers what each action id asked for,
and the receipt half connects a wallet because Portfolio needs one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: hostile-operator.mjs — six books from an operator that lies

Missing fields, negative and absurd numbers, wrong types, HTML in strings,
a cleared auction with no winner, a response that is not an array. Two of
the six white-screened the desk. Removing the required-field check brings
one straight back.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: drive the disclosure, and stop the suite eating its own auction

The live branch now builds a disclosure from the stored seal, verifies it,
and tampers with the amount to check it is refused — the step that found
both of today's bugs.

Two things that made the suite unrepeatable, both mine:
- It always bid on the first SEALED row, so a second run hit "already
  sealed" and read that as a broken seal. It skips rows marked BID SEALED,
  after waiting for those markers to arrive.
- " 12 " was in the wrong-path list. The desk trims before it parses, so a
  padded number is a VALID bid — and it sealed one, which made the honest
  bid that followed the second from that address. A right-path value in a
  wrong-path list does not just under-test; it breaks what comes after.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: a wallet on the wrong chain, and a build that matches what deploys

Two checks in a second browser context, because a wallet's chain is fixed
when it is installed: a wallet on chain 1 must be told so before it bids,
and the desk must name the chain it is actually on.

And the note that matters for every local run: .env.local bakes a
localhost proxy into `npm run build`, so the dist being checked was not
the dist that deploys — and the no-polling check was skipped every single
time because of it. Build with VITE_TEE_PROXY_URL= and it runs: 84 checks
rather than 81.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: pixel baselines for the desk, and a name for them

visual.mjs derived the baseline name from the hostname, so anything served
locally was called "localhost" and two pages would overwrite each other's
baselines. --name= instead.

Four viewports, light and dark, stable at 0.005% between runs. Changing
the accent token fails all four.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: follow the post form to minutes and the two clearing shapes

Also fixes a check that had gone quiet: fillByLabel("Deadline block")
returns false rather than throwing when the label is gone, so the renamed
field was simply never filled.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: decide "is this desk live" from whether an enclave answered

The demo-banner check read the banner to decide whether to check the
banner: the desk was asked to admit it was on demo data, and the evidence
for the question was the admission itself. It now watches for a successful
/direct response and asserts both directions — a desk with no enclave must
say the book is a demo, a desk with one must not.

Two more that passed by accident: "selecting an auction changes the page"
clicked the row the desk had already selected, and the live-flow hint was
asserted against a stack that is live and therefore does not show it.

And the disclosure round trip: seal a bid, find the receipt in Portfolio,
click it, and the nonce field holds 32 bytes nobody typed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: the post form, reopened between attempts

A post that succeeds closes the form and goes back to the book, which is
right and which the garbage-input loop did not expect: against a live
enclave the first click really does post, and every attempt after it timed
out on a field that was no longer there. The whole suite now runs green
against a real backend with a connected wallet — 77 checks, including the
branch that seals a valid bid and reads the receipt.

Plus checks for the activity panel.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: pin the commitment list, the panel headings and the countdown

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: follow the desk's new structure

The cleared-auction checks now expect the receipt that opens under the
row. And the button loop walks the sidebar, so it ends wherever the last
nav item it clicked leads — Audit, where there is no book at all. Navigate
back deliberately instead of assuming a click loop left the desk somewhere
useful.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: follow the desk to /dashboard and the landing into frontend/

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: check the desk is usable before anything is clicked

Six checks that run on load: the bid form is there without a selection,
the desk did not open on a closed auction, the counts are stated, posting
is offered with nothing selected, and a cleared auction explains itself
and offers a next move instead of stopping.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

check the submission's on-chain claims instead of trusting them

The proof table is nothing but public reads — transaction hashes, Flare's
own contract addresses, a tag reservation — and all of it can go stale
without a line of code changing. The addresses in particular are Flare's:
writing one down is a claim about the ContractRegistry, so ask the
registry rather than trust the markdown.

Eleven claims: every hash in the table succeeded (taking them all means a
new row is checked when it is written, not when someone remembers to add
it here), each named contract matches what the registry resolves,
destination tag 205 is still reserved, and an allowed executor is set for
it. Corrupting one address and one hash fails exactly those two.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: the default target resolved to a directory that does not exist

new URL(...).pathname percent-encodes the space in "Flare Hackathon", so
running flows-landing.mjs or render.mjs with no argument served an empty
page. flows-landing then died on a 30s locator timeout rather than a
failed check, which is the worse failure: a crash reads as a broken
harness, not as a page that never loaded.

fileURLToPath instead. 19 checks pass again.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

qa: a test wallet, and the bug it found on the first run

Every desk wrong-path ended at "connect a wallet", so the half of the app
behind that button had never been run by anything but a person.
qa/wallet.mjs injects an EIP-1193 provider: the page holds no key, calls
cross to node over one exposed function, viem signs there, reads go to the
public Coston2 RPC and eth_sendTransaction refuses on purpose.

It found the bug immediately. The bid amount is parsed with BigInt, and
the parse sat outside the try — "abc", "1.5" and "1e9" each threw an
uncaught SyntaxError, so the button did nothing and the desk said nothing.
Now the amount is checked before it is parsed, and eight values are typed
into the field on every run.

Two of my own checks were inert and are fixed with it: the button loop
clicked the account control, which opened a modal that swallowed every
click after it, and the no-polling check measured its window after a bid
had already posted to /direct — so it read "a proxy is configured" against
the deployed build, which has none.

58 checks, 0 failed against production.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

prove.ts: pull the verdict out of the script so it can be tested

prove.ts fetched, decoded and printed at the top level, so the part a
merchant would actually act on — who gets the FXRP, what survives the
fees, when it lands — was the only part with no test. Extracted it to
describe(), which takes the proof, the limiter snapshot and whatever the
tag manager returned, and returns the judgement. The script now only
fetches.

Four tests, three mutations killed: crediting the gross instead of the
net, trusting a registered recipient on a payment with no tag, and
calling a below-minimum payment mintable.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Assert the distinction the desk now draws, not the wording it used to have

The check demanded "EXTENSION OFFLINE", which was the thing being fixed — so it
failed the moment the better version deployed. That is the check working, but
the assertion had pinned a symptom rather than the property.

It now allows either state and forbids the contradiction: the page may say the
TEE is in production, or that the extension is offline, never both.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Compare the dark palette too, and mask the line that would have gone stale

The page defines a full dark palette under prefers-color-scheme and the check
forced light, so half of it was never compared — a colour that stopped
resolving in dark mode would have looked perfectly fine. Four baselines now,
both themes at both widths, all stable at 0.000%.

Also masked #customer-line, added an hour ago. It carries a figure derived from
the live FTSO price, so it was going to start failing tomorrow for the market's
reasons rather than the page's. That is the third time content has drifted into
this check; the rule is worth stating plainly — anything showing a live number
belongs in the volatile list the moment it is added.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Tell the customer when it arrives, on the page as well as the CLI

estimate.ts was wired into the checkout command and nowhere a customer looks.
The dashboard's invoice panel showed every deduction and said nothing about
time, which is the question a spinner exists to avoid answering.

Two flow checks guard it, and the second is the one that matters: the line must
never say "instant" or "immediately". Executing immediately is a fact about the
limiter — the FDC round trip is 150 seconds on our own measurement, so a page
that implies instant is wrong about the only thing the customer cares about.

It clears on invalid input alongside the table, because a promise about delivery
is exactly the kind of stale answer worth nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Prune finished payments, and never unfinished ones

One file per payment is the right shape and it grows without end. all() reads
every file on every --report, so the cost is paid on each call rather than once.

--prune drops finished payments older than thirty days. The safety argument is
the whole feature: an unfinished entry still holds a proof we paid for, so
removing it would make the next tick buy another. It is therefore never
eligible, however old — a payment stuck for a month is a bug to look at, not
rubbish to sweep up. An entry with no timestamp is kept rather than guessed at.

Three tests, including the one that matters: an old unfinished payment survives
a prune with its request intact.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Give TagRail the "do not trust us" script Buta already had

Undelayed quotes more on-chain evidence than Buta and had no way for a sceptic
to check any of it. npm run status prints every claim the submission makes about
the rail — the fee model, the stale-getter discrepancy the whole product exists
to remove, what a customer would be told right now, and the receipt of our bot's
winning transaction — all from public reads, with no key.

The first version hand-wrote function selectors and printed "registry lookup
failed" on the very first line. That was the right failure: a guessed selector
is a way to print a confident wrong number, which is the opposite of what a
verification script is for. It reads through src/chain.ts now, so if the script
is right the product is too, and neither can drift from the other.

It caught a live one on the first real run: the hourly getter reports 2.15 XRP
used in a window that has already rolled over. Actual usage is zero.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Publish a record a merchant could choose an executor on

totals() answers "was this worth running" for the operator. This answers the
question somebody else asks: should I point my tag at you?

npm run bot -- --publish writes finalised, lost races, outstanding, win rate and
tags served. Two decisions in it. The losses are included, because a record that
only lists wins is an advert rather than evidence. And an empty record reports a
null win rate rather than 0% or 100% — a rate computed from no data is a claim,
and the point of the file is to be checkable.

Outstanding payments are in it too: a payment seen and not finished is a cost to
the merchant even when it costs the executor nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Test the window-alignment assertion that could not be reached

readLimits asserts the on-chain window start is a multiple of the window size,
because HOUR and DAY are assumptions — the contract never exposes them. If that
assumption is ever wrong, every prediction after it is quietly wrong too, so the
assertion is load-bearing. It was inline in a network-bound function, where
nothing could test it.

assertAligned is exported now, and refuses a zero window size rather than
dividing by it. Six tests also cover ask() and capacityUba(), including the
granularity case: with granularity 1000 a 150,000 XRP payment is 150 AMG, far
below a threshold expressed in AMG, so treating UBA as AMG would call it large.

My own fixture was misaligned on the first run, which is the failure the
assertion exists to catch — it caught mine.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Make the documents fail the build when they lie

Every count in the README was maintained by hand, and twice this session one was
quietly wrong: it claimed 15 tests when there were 53, and 17 parity vectors when
there were 217. Nobody noticed, because a stale number reads exactly like a fresh
one. A judge who checks one claim and finds it wrong stops believing the rest.

test/docs.test.ts counts the tests that exist, counts the committed vectors, and
compares both against what the documents say. It also checks that every module
the README lists is actually there, and that no placeholder survived into the
submission.

It earned its place on the first run: 53 vs 80 tests, and 17 vs 217 scenarios.
Both corrected.

Also dropped bot-state.coston2.json. It was imported into the ledger days ago and
keeping a second source of truth around only invites someone to read the wrong
one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Answer the question the spinner dodges

A checkout shows a spinner because the integrator has nothing better to say.
Everything needed for a real answer was already here: the limiter replay knows
when execution is allowed, and the FDC round trip has a measured floor.

src/estimate.ts puts them together and the checkout prints the result —
"23.65 FXRP arrives in a few minutes", or "149,624.9 FXRP arrives in about 2
hours (large mintings are delayed by protocol)".

Two rules, both tested. It rounds up: an hour and two minutes described as
"about an hour" is a promise that has already expired by the time it is read. And
"allowed immediately" is a fact about the limiter, not about the customer's wait
— the FDC round trip is 150 seconds on our own measurement, so nothing here is
ever called instant.

A payment below the minimum fee is reported as a rejection rather than a wait,
because no amount of waiting will mint it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Make the split panel deterministic instead of hiding it

Hiding #split-wrap stopped the flakiness and cost the check its subject: the
split table was then never compared at all. Avoiding a problem is not fixing it.

The panel appears only when the mint is delayed, and whether 120,000 XRP is
delayed depends on the live limiter. An amount at or above the large-mint
threshold is always delayed, whatever the limiter says — so the simulator is put
in that state before the screenshot, the panel is always present, and it is
always in frame. Three consecutive runs at 0.000%.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

The roadmap listed two things that already shipped

A roadmap that promises work already done reads as either careless or padded,
and it undersells the submission either way.

The shared ledger runs several executor processes without buying the same proof
twice and totals the books across them, so "executor as a service" is now about
the part that is genuinely missing: a published record a merchant could choose
on. And --split sends the pieces rather than only planning them — what has never
happened is a split above the 100,000 XRP cliff, because the faucet does not
reach it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Pin the one panel whose presence depends on the chain

The visual check failed at 0.32% overnight, and it was right to flag it and
wrong about the cause: #split-wrap only appears when the simulated mint is
currently delayed, which depends on the live limiter state. So its presence
moves a few thousand pixels for the chain's reasons rather than the page's.

Hidden for the screenshot. Whether it appears at all is a behaviour, and the
flow checks already assert it — a small mint shows no split, a mint over the
cliff shows two pieces. Four consecutive runs now agree at 0.000%.

That is three flakiness sources found by using this thing rather than by
reasoning about it: content length, panel presence, and the initial mistake of
hiding the very sections that carry the colour.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Pixel diff, and a ledger that lets more than one executor run

Two of the four asked for. Both had a first version that quietly did nothing,
which is becoming the pattern worth naming: a check that passes without
exercising anything reads exactly like a check that passes.

The pixel diff compares screenshots against committed baselines, with no image
library — Chromium already decodes PNG, so the comparison runs on a canvas in a
blank page. It catches what the DOM cannot: a colour token that stops resolving,
a font that fails to subset, a border that vanishes. Proven by changing the
accent colour, which moved 2.7% of the desktop pixels while render and flow
checks stayed clean.

The first version hid every panel holding live numbers. Those are also the panels
holding the accent colour, the rules and most of the type, so the colour
mutation moved exactly zero pixels. Volatile text is overwritten now, not
hidden. The second version overwrote it with a filler the same length as the
original, which made the check flaky instead of inert: a chain number growing
from five digits to seven moved real pixels. It is a fixed-length filler now,
and two consecutive runs agree.

src/ledger.ts replaces the single JSON state file. One process was fine; two —
one per tag, or a restart draining alongside its replacement — is a way to lose
money. Both read the file, both see no attestation for a payment, both buy one;
and whichever saves second erases the other's record of a proof it already paid
for, so it gets bought a third time. One file per payment now, and the claim IS
the file's creation: `wx` fails if the path exists, atomically, on every
platform. A crashed worker's claim is taken over after ten minutes, keeping the
request it paid for. The old state file is imported once, so upgrading does not
re-buy everything.

Nine ledger tests, including the takeover keeping the proof, books adding up
across workers, and a transaction id that tries to escape the directory.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Test the executor sequence that costs money, and fix the key I just broke

Two rules in the bot's loop had no test, and both are paid for in gas. A proof
is bought once and reused across every later attempt, so an executor returning
an hour later for a delayed minting does not buy a second one. And a lost race
is over — PaymentAlreadyConfirmed means someone else finalised it, the merchant
has their FXRP, and retrying pays gas forever for a call that can never succeed.

attempt.ts takes its dependencies as arguments, so seven tests pin the sequence
without a chain: the order of operations, that the request is saved *before* the
proof is fetched (a request paid for and forgotten is paid for twice), that a
delay keeps the proof it already bought, and that the fee recorded is the one
the split actually pays rather than the setting.

The Entry shape now has one definition instead of two copies waiting to drift.

Also: yesterday's DIRECT_API_KEY change broke the documented local dev path.
frontend/.env.example still told developers to use test-api-key-change-me, which
the proxy now refuses.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Fill the desk's forms, and stop the wallet modal from hiding an empty test

Clicking buttons proves they do not throw. Filling the forms proves the desk
refuses for a reason it can state — and it does: posting a block with no wallet
connected opens the wallet prompt rather than doing nothing.

That prompt is also what broke the first version of this test. The modal covers
the page, so the five iterations after the first were clicking an overlay and
passing without testing anything. It is closed between iterations now, and each
one asserts the field actually holds what was typed, so a fill that silently
failed cannot masquerade as a form that handled it.

27 checks on the desk, 19 on the landing demo, 60 on the dashboard.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Exercise the landing page's sealed-bid demo, which nothing had ever clicked

render.mjs loads the page and checks it is not visibly broken. It never presses
Clear, so it could not tell whether the demo demonstrates anything — and that
demo is the argument the whole page makes.

Nineteen checks: the book starts sealed with five bids and no price, clearing
reveals exactly one winner and leaves the other four sealed with no amount

Undelayed: predict when a FAssets direct minting actually executes

FAssets direct minting does not fail when it hits a rate limit — it goes quiet
and executes later. The XRP is already at the core vault and the payment is
already recorded, so integrators either send a second payment or retry early,
revert DirectMintingStillDelayed and burn the FDC proof they paid for.

Reading the chain does not save you. The limiter is not a tumbling window: each
elapsed window subtracts one whole limit instead of resetting, so overspend
carries forward and allowedAt = windowStart + windowSize * minted / max. The
state getters return raw AMG while the limit getters convert to UBA. A mint at
or above the large-mint threshold skips both limiters and consumes no quota at
all. On a quiet Coston2 afternoon the daily getter reported 16,285 XRP used
against a window that had expired 26 hours earlier.

This replays the limiter off-chain exactly as the contract runs it, and answers
the one question every integrator has. Plus TagRail, the merchant half: reserve
a tag in Flare's own MintingTagManager — we did not write that contract and are
not going to — show the core vault address and the tag at checkout, and let an
executor bot prove the payment and finalise it for the fee.

Proven on Coston2: tag 205 reserved, a 5 XRP payment carrying it, 4.8 FTestXRP
at the merchant address. A competing executor won that first race, so our call
reverted PaymentAlreadyConfirmed and our proof fee was wasted; that finding is
left in, because it is the clearest statement of why knowing the timing is
worth anything. With the tag's allowedExecutor set, the second payment was ours:
7 XRP in, 0.1 system fee, 6.8 to the merchant, 0.1 executor fee to the bot.

parity/ holds the verified MintingRateLimiter.sol byte for byte and checks the
TypeScript against what it actually did across 17 scenarios, rather than
against anyone's reading of it.
